source_text: Convertor ad alios aeque sibi prudentes, qui carnem Christi animalem affirmant, quod anima caro sit facta, ergo et caro anima, et sicut caro animalis, ita et anima carnalis. Et hic itaque causas requiro. Si, ut animam salvam faceret, in semetipso suscepit animam Christus, quia salva non esset nisi per ipsum, dum in ipso, non video cur eam carnem fecerit animalem induendo carnem, quasi aliter animam salvam facere non posset, nisi carnem factam. Cum enim nostras animas non tantum non carneas, sed etiam a carne disiunctas salvas praestet, quanto magis illum, quam ipse suscepit, etiam non carneam redigere potuit in salutem? Item cum praesumant non carnis, sed animae nostrae solius liberandae causa processisse Christum, primo quam absurdum est ut animam solam liberaturus id genus corporis eam fecerit quod non erat liberaturus? Deinde si animas nostras per illam, quam gestavit, liberare susceperat, illam quoque, quam gestavit, nostram gestasse debuerat, id est nostrae formae, cuiuscunque formae est in occulto anima nostra, non tamen carneae. Ceterum non nostram animam liberavit, si carneam habuit; nostra enim carnea non est. Porro si non nostram liberavit, quia carneam liberavit, nihil ad nos, quia non nostram liberavit. Sed nec liberanda erat, quae non erat nostra, ut scilicet carnea. Non enim periclitabatur, si non erat nostra, id est non carnea, Sed liberatam constat illam. Ergo non fuit carnea, et fuit nostra, si ea fuit quae liberaretur, quoniam periclitabatur. Iam ergo si anima non fuit carnalis in Christo, nec caro potest animalis fuisse.
thought_title: Against the view that Christ's flesh was made of soul
orientation: Tertullian has just argued that Christ's flesh was earthly, not heavenly; now he turns to those who say Christ's flesh was made of soul, and asks why Christ would have made the soul flesh if he came to save the soul.
pass_a_gloss: I turn to others equally wise in their own eyes, who affirm that the flesh of Christ was made of soul, because the soul was made flesh, therefore also the flesh was made soul, and just as the flesh was made of soul, so also the soul was made fleshly. And here too I ask for reasons. If, in order to make the soul safe, Christ took up a soul in himself, because it would not be safe except through him, while it was in him, I do not see why he made it fleshly by putting on flesh, as if he could not otherwise make the soul safe, except by making it flesh. For since he makes our souls safe, which are not only not fleshly but also separated from flesh, how much more could he bring that soul, which he himself took up, even not fleshly, into safety? Likewise, since they presume that Christ came forth for the purpose of freeing not the flesh but our soul alone, first, how absurd is it that he who was going to free the soul alone made it that kind of body which he was not going to free? Then, if he had undertaken to free our souls through that soul which he bore, he ought also to have borne that soul which he bore as ours, that is, of our form, whatever form our soul is in secret, but not fleshly. Otherwise he did not free our soul, if he had a fleshly one; for ours is not fleshly. Further, if he did not free ours, because he freed a fleshly one, it is nothing to us, because he did not free ours. But neither was that soul which was not ours to be freed, namely as fleshly. For it was not in danger, if it was not ours, that is, not fleshly. But it is established that that soul was freed. Therefore it was not fleshly, and it was ours, if it was that soul which was freed, since it was in danger. Now therefore, if the soul was not fleshly in Christ, neither could the flesh have been made of soul.

choices.why: The glossary bans 'animal' and 'soulish'; 'made of soul' preserves the heretical sense that Christ's flesh was soul-substance.
The glossary bans 'carnality' but not 'fleshly'; it keeps the adjectival force of carnalis distinct from the noun caro.
The glossary bans 'save' only for resurrectio terms; 'make safe' renders salvam facere literally and avoids theological flattening.
Libero is distinct from salvum facio; 'to be freed' keeps the literal force of liberation rather than salvation.
The verb means 'to be at risk'; 'was in danger' is literal and preserves the argument that only a soul like ours was endangered.

pass_b_english: I turn now to others who are equally wise in their own eyes: those who claim that Christ's flesh was made of soul, because the soul became flesh, and therefore the flesh became soul, and just as the flesh was made of soul, so the soul was fleshly. Here too I ask for their reasons. If Christ took up a soul into himself in order to make the soul safe, because it could not be made safe except through him while it was in him, I do not see why by putting on flesh he made it flesh made of soul, as if he could not make the soul safe in any other way unless it became flesh. For since he makes our souls safe even though they are not only not fleshly but also separated from flesh, how much more could he have brought that soul which he himself took up to safety even without making it fleshly? Again, since they presume that Christ came for the purpose of freeing not our flesh but our soul alone, first, how absurd it is that he who was going to free the soul alone made it into the kind of body he was not going to free. Then, if he had undertaken to free our souls through that soul which he bore, he ought to have borne a soul like ours as well—that is, of our form, whatever form our soul has in its hidden state, but certainly not fleshly. Otherwise he did not free our soul, if the soul he had was fleshly; for ours is not fleshly. Further, if he did not free our soul because he freed a fleshly one, that has nothing to do with us, because he did not free our soul. But neither did a soul that was not ours need to be freed—that is, a fleshly one. For it was not in danger if it was not ours, that is, not fleshly. But it is agreed that it was freed. Therefore it was not fleshly, and it was ours, if it was the soul that was freed, since it was in danger. Now then, if the soul in Christ was not fleshly, neither could the flesh have been made of soul.

problems.quote: why he made it fleshly by putting on flesh
problems.source_quote: cur eam carnem fecerit animalem induendo carnem
problems.why: carnem animalem means flesh made of soul, not carnalis (fleshly). The predicate that drives the argument is lost.
problems.fix: why, by putting on flesh, he made that soul into flesh made of soul
problems.ruling: Source: "carnem fecerit animalem" = made the flesh animalis (soul-made); English "made it fleshly" reverses subject/predicate, confusing the opponents' soul-flesh claim and breaking the argument.

edits.old: why he made it fleshly by putting on flesh
edits.new: why by putting on flesh he made it flesh made of soul

fixed: Fixed 'made it fleshly' to 'made it flesh made of soul' for source 'eam carnem fecerit animalem induendo carnem', where animalem means made of soul, not fleshly.
